doc.title: Charles McPherson interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 9, 2024 [interview 2 of 2]

title: How he wrote the tune and the players' reaction
summary: He wrote it like a boxed-in solo; Wong and Patton found it tricky but nailed it.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Indeed. And I’m picturing you, were you sitting at the piano laboriously writing out this [scats]-type line?
Is that how you did it?

Yeah. Basically yeah. I actually basically it’s really kind of like a solo I would do. And of course I have a way of — what would you say — framing it a certain way so that there © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

are certain nuances being adhered to that will make it not just a solo but a tune, and there’s a way that you can — I use the term “box it” or conceptualize certain phrasing and melodic nuance and a way that you maybe recapitulate to some degree here or there that makes it not just a rambling solo but actually a little tune. And so I’ve tried to do the best I could trying to do that. Yeah.
I bet they were happy to see it. I’m just picturing —

No they weren’t that happy. I don’t know if they were happy to see it because they had to really — they had to — I mean it’s pretty notey, you know there’s a lot of notes there and so, and it’s in unison and the rhythm is kind of tricky a little bit. It’s just based on “I Got Rhythm” but you know the line is not real easy. Now I’ve seen other people look at that and not want to deal with it so — yeah but these two guys are so talented, David Wong and Jeb Patton, that they — I mean for them it’s a challenge and they ate it up. They nailed it for sure.
And I just want to compliment you on the idea of the formatting of it, even up to the end where it’s sort of a surprise ending.
